one_liner: Header-only C++20/23 coroutine fork-join library beating oneTBB and OpenMP on fine-grained task throughput and memory.
what_it_does: libfork is a fine-grained fork-join task-parallelism library: you write async functions as lambdas/functors returning lf::task<T> and spawn children with co_await lf::fork/lf::call, then co_await lf::join before reading results. Tasks run on a scheduler (lazy_pool, busy_pool, or unit_pool) started via lf::sync_wait(pool, fn, args...), which blocks the calling thread until the pool finishes. It is not a drop-in replacement for oneTBB's task_group or OpenMP pragmas; existing recursive functions must be rewritten as C++20 coroutines.
how_it_is_fast: A continuation-stealing work-stealing scheduler lets the worker that forks a task keep running the child immediately while only the continuation is exposed to be stolen, minimizing deque traffic on the common path. Coroutine frames are placed on an (almost) non-allocating 'cactus stack' built from segmented stacks instead of being heap-allocated per task, giving fork/call overhead about 10x a bare function call. NUMA-aware pools (optionally using hwloc for topology detection) reduce cross-socket stealing cost, which the paper credits for near-linear time and memory scaling up to 112 cores.
when_to_use: Very fine-grained recursive divide-and-conquer workloads (fib-style, tree search, numerical integration) where oneTBB/OpenMP per-task overhead dominates runtime
Codebases willing to rewrite hot-path functions as C++20 coroutines (lf::task<T>) rather than keep existing std::async/TBB/OpenMP call sites unchanged
Multi-socket/NUMA machines with high core counts (paper benchmarked 1-112 cores, 2 NUMA nodes) where linear time/memory scaling matters
Workloads where peak RSS is as important as speed - libfork's memory footprint was measured far below TBB/OpenMP/Taskflow on the UTS tree-search benchmark
Projects that can pin a recent compiler (current main requires C++23 per CMakeLists) via CMake, vcpkg, or Conan
when_not_to_use: Any deployment target still on MSVC: BUILDING.md states libfork compiles on MSVC 19.35-19.37 but seg-faults at runtime due to an open Visual Studio symmetric-transfer/coroutine codegen bug

Coarser-grained parallel loops: a real integration into BLIS's GEMM (issue #113) showed libfork's busy_pool at only 55% of OpenMP's GFLOPS at matrix dim=512, only beating OpenMP once dim >= 2048, partly because libfork lacks a flat bulk-spawn/parallel_invoke API
Teams unwilling to convert call sites to coroutine-returning lf::task<T> and to handle its exception_before_join + rethrow-on-join exception model

Older/unpatched compilers: Clang <=16 needs a thread_local workaround with a performance penalty, and GCC below -O2 can stack-overflow because it doesn't guarantee coroutine symmetric-transfer tail calls

Anyone requiring peer-reviewed evidence: the only performance writeup is an arXiv v1 preprint (Feb 2024) with no journal/conference publication, and its headline 'up to' ratios are peak fib/integrate figures at 112 cores, well above the abstract's stated averages (2.7x/7.2x)

integration.dependencies: none required beyond a compiler and Threads; optional hwloc >=2.5.0 for NUMA topology detection (LF_USE_HWLOC)
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 per docs (C++23 preferred); current main CMakeLists.txt sets target_compile_features(... cxx_std_23) on the library interface target. Compiler support table: Clang 15-18 (16 and below need a thread_local workaround with a perf penalty due to LLVM bugs #63022/#47179), GCC 11-13 (needs >= -O2 for guaranteed coroutine tail calls), Apple Clang (Xcode-shipped, with the same old-Clang mitigations), MSVC 19.35-19.37 compiles but seg-faults at runtime
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows CI configured (linux.yml/macos.yml/windows.yml), any arch with a conforming C++20/23 coroutine compiler; NUMA-aware scheduling is opt-in via hwloc
integration.thread_safety: not documented as a single formal guarantee; README describes the core as 'lock-free, wait-free, continuation-stealing'; schedulers (lazy_pool/busy_pool) are multi-threaded work-stealing pools meant for concurrent task submission, and lf::sync_wait blocks the calling thread until the pool drains
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false - requires rewriting functions as C++20 coroutines returning lf::task<T> using lf::fork/lf::call/lf::join instead of oneTBB task_group calls or OpenMP pragmas

gotchas: Strict fork-join is enforced: every forked/called child must be joined with co_await lf::join before the parent task returns - there is no fire-and-forget

Exceptions from a child surfaced before the join point arrive as exception_before_join; you must catch it and still call join, which then rethrows the child's real exception (include/libfork/core/exceptions.hpp)
Current main branch requires C++23 (cxx_std_23 in CMakeLists.txt) even though the README/BUILDING.md prose still advertises 'C++20 coroutines' - check your compiler before adopting HEAD
MSVC builds compile but crash at runtime (known upstream MSVC coroutine codegen bug); do not ship an MSVC build without testing
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick libfork over TooManyCooks/dispenso/Taskflow when the workload is extremely fine-grained recursive fork-join (fib-like or UTS-style tree search) run across dozens to 100+ cores and peak memory matters as much as latency; TMC and dispenso report comparable 'beats oneTBB' wins with a simpler non-coroutine API and less compiler sensitivity, so prefer them if you don't want to rewrite call sites as C++20/23 coroutines or can't guarantee a modern compiler.
verified_claims_summary: The arXiv:2402.18480 preprint (Williams & Elliott) benchmarked libfork 3.5.0 against oneTBB 2021.10.0, Clang-bundled OpenMP/libomp, and Taskflow 3.6.0 on fib(42), integration, matmul, nqueens(14), and UTS tree-search, compiled with Clang 18.0.0 at the paper's 'highest optimization setting,' on 2x Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+ (112 cores, 2 NUMA nodes, 500GiB RAM), swept from 1-112 cores. Abstract-stated averages are 2.7x faster / 6.2x less memory than oneTBB and 7.2x faster / 10x less memory than OpenMP; the frequently quoted 7.5x/19x (vs TBB) and 24x/24x (vs OpenMP) figures are peak ratios on the fib benchmark specifically at 112 cores, not typical-case numbers.
status_note: Actively maintained - default-branch last commit 2026-01-17 - and header-only/copyable under MPL-2.0, so it can be vendored without a package manager, but current HEAD needs a C++23-capable compiler, MSVC support is presently broken at runtime, and the last tagged release (v3.8.0) is from 2024-05-10 with substantial unreleased work since.
